paragraphs: Training a neural network involves searching for parameters that make its loss small. The difficulty is that the loss can have an irregular shape: a parameter setting may look best compared with nearby settings while still being worse than a solution elsewhere. Such a setting is a bad local minimum. This paper examines whether a small architectural change can remove these traps for binary classification.

The authors prove that, under mild assumptions, adding one specially constructed neuron with a direct connection to the output makes every local minimum a global minimum. They also establish this property for an alternative modification that adds a special neuron to each layer. The result concerns these particular constructions, rather than an arbitrary extra neuron.

The significance is that a small change in architecture can fundamentally alter the optimization landscape. The guarantee identifies the quality of local minima under the stated assumptions; it does not itself establish that a training procedure will reach one. Its contribution is a conditional mathematical route to eliminating suboptimal local minima.
neurips-2018-adding-one-neuron-can-elimi.tldr: Under mild assumptions, adding specially constructed neurons to a binary classifier makes every local minimum globally optimal.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization speeds up learning by asking several machines to estimate gradients at each iteration. This paper considers an adversarial version of that arrangement: an alpha fraction of the m machines can behave arbitrarily instead of providing trustworthy estimates. Ordinary mini-batch stochastic gradient descent benefits from more machines, but does not tolerate these Byzantine failures.

The authors develop an SGD variant for convex objectives that reaches an epsilon-approximate minimum in roughly 1/(epsilon² m) + alpha²/epsilon² iterations, ignoring logarithmic factors. The first term captures the familiar benefit of distributing work. The second expresses the additional cost associated with the adversarial fraction. Consequently, increasing the number of machines reduces one component of the bound while leaving the corruption-related component.

A matching lower bound shows that, up to logarithmic factors, the method is information-theoretically optimal in sample and time complexity. This makes the result more than a robustness construction: it characterizes how much optimization efficiency must be sacrificed to tolerate adversarial workers in the studied convex setting.
neurips-2018-byzantine-stochastic-gradie.tldr: A Byzantine-tolerant SGD variant achieves near-optimal sample and time complexity for distributed convex optimization.

paragraphs: Clebsch–Gordan Nets address learning from spherical images while making the result insensitive to rotations. The paper builds on an earlier approach that used group representation theory and noncommutative harmonic analysis to achieve strong results on this problem. Its contribution is a generalization that the authors describe as both generally better performing and simpler to implement.

The central architectural choice is to use the Clebsch–Gordan transform as the network’s only source of nonlinearity. Nonlinearity lets a network express relationships beyond those available through linear operations alone. Here, that capability is incorporated into a network operating entirely in Fourier space, avoiding repeated forward and backward Fourier transforms.

This matters because the reported performance improvement comes alongside a simpler implementation, rather than requiring repeated changes of representation. The performance claim is qualified as a general tendency, not a guarantee for every case. The authors also state that the underlying ideas extend to networks invariant under other compact groups, giving the approach relevance beyond rotations of spherical images.
neurips-2018-clebschgordan-nets-a-fully-.tldr: Clebsch–Gordan Nets use a single kind of nonlinear transform to learn rotation-invariant spherical images entirely in Fourier space, with generally improved performance and simpler implementation.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels are especially troublesome for deep networks because their capacity allows them to eventually memorize those errors. Co-teaching builds on the observation that networks tend to learn examples with clean labels before fitting examples with noisy labels. The method uses this difference in learning behavior to guide which examples contribute to training.

Two networks train simultaneously. For each mini-batch, both first process all examples and select a subset whose labels may be clean. They then exchange their selections. Each network updates its parameters using the examples chosen by the other network, so the selection decision and the resulting update are distributed across the pair.

The selected labels are only potentially clean; the procedure does not require that its judgments be infallible. Experiments on noisy versions of MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 report substantially stronger robustness than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The central contribution is a concrete way to turn early learning behavior into cooperative example selection, helping training remain useful when supplied labels contain extensive errors.
neurips-2018-co-teaching-robust-training.tldr: Co-teaching trains two networks on examples selected by each other to improve robustness to noisy labels.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several causal networks indistinguishable because different edge directions may encode the same observational relationships. This paper uses interventions to resolve causal structure through path queries. A query asks whether one variable can reach another along directed edges, and is answered by intervening on the origin variable and sampling the target.

The authors first give a polynomial-time algorithm that recovers the correctly oriented transitive reduction with high probability. This reduction preserves directed reachability while removing edges made redundant by other paths. For both continuous and discrete networks, they establish logarithmic sample complexity for the interventional data needed by each path query.

They then recover the additional transitive edges to obtain the full network, again with logarithmic sample complexity. For discrete networks, this stage takes time exponential in the maximum number of parents, separating statistical efficiency from computational cost. The paper also reduces the number of queries for rooted trees and analyzes imperfect interventions. Together, these results make intervention-based reachability a useful intermediate step toward recovering complete causal structure.
neurips-2018-computationally-and-statist.tldr: Interventional path queries enable efficient recovery of causal reachability and, with additional computation, the full network.

paragraphs: Structured prediction treats related output variables jointly, as in semantic segmentation, where predictions across an image have useful relationships. Encoding those correlations supplies prior information that can reduce the data needs of deep networks. Existing deep structured models, however, often restrict interactions to small neighborhoods because larger structures are computationally expensive.

A second restriction concerns what happens after a structured output or its representation has been produced. Many formulations cannot apply further nonlinear transformations to it. Recent approaches insert graphical model inference inside a deep network to permit such processing, but their optimization is challenging and remains insufficiently understood. The paper addresses this combination of representational and optimization difficulties.

The authors develop a model that generalizes existing approaches, including structured prediction energy networks. They also discuss a formulation that preserves the applicability of existing inference techniques. Its contribution is a broader framework for combining structured relationships with nonlinear output processing while retaining access to established inference machinery. This matters because richer output representations must still support the computations needed to make predictions.
neurips-2018-deep-structured-prediction-.tldr: A generalized deep structured model supports nonlinear output transformations while preserving applicability of existing inference techniques.

paragraphs: Interactive image search can improve results by asking users for feedback, but a yes-or-no judgment or a fixed menu of attributes limits what they can communicate. This paper lets users describe their preferences in natural language over successive dialog turns. The search system can therefore use more expressive feedback when moving toward a target image.

The authors formulate the dialog as reinforcement learning. At each turn, the system receives a reward for improving the target image's rank. Because collecting human conversations throughout training would be costly, they train with a simulated user. That simulator learns to describe differences between a candidate image and the target, supplying feedback for the retrieval system's learning process.

Experiments in footwear retrieval use both simulated and real-world data. The proposed framework achieves better accuracy than the compared supervised and reinforcement learning baselines. Natural-language feedback also produces more effective retrieval than predefined attributes. These results support both the learning framework and the choice of an expressive conversational interface within the evaluated application.
neurips-2018-dialog-based-interactive-im.tldr: A retrieval system trained through simulated dialog uses natural-language feedback to improve footwear image search.

paragraphs: A contextual linear bandit repeatedly chooses an action using information supplied for the current round, then observes a stochastic reward. The context may be arbitrary or adversarial, while the reward follows the assumed feature-based model. This paper asks how such a learner can protect users' information while still making effective sequential decisions.

The authors show that standard differential privacy leads to linear regret in this setting. They instead adopt joint differential privacy: the action for a user is revealed only to that user, while subsequent outputs must protect that user's information. This changes the privacy requirement to reflect who can actually see each action.

The paper gives a general conversion of linear-UCB into a jointly private algorithm using a tree-based mechanism. It develops versions using Gaussian or Wishart noise and bounds their regret. A further lower bound establishes an unavoidable additional regret cost for private multi-armed bandit algorithms. Together, the results connect the visibility of decisions, the privacy definition, and the price paid in learning performance.
neurips-2018-differentially-private-cont.tldr: Joint differential privacy enables contextual linear bandit algorithms with regret guarantees under a user-specific action-visibility assumption.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent must explore enough to discover useful behavior before settling on a policy. That is difficult when there are many possible states, rewards are rare, or apparently promising behavior leads to an inferior local optimum. This paper introduces an exploration strategy that makes diversity an explicit part of the learning objective.

The method adds a distance measure to the loss function to encourage more exploratory behavior. It can be combined with both on-policy and off-policy algorithms, making it applicable across different training arrangements. The authors also introduce adaptive scaling to stabilize learning, addressing how the additional exploration term interacts with the rest of the optimization.

Experiments cover large two-dimensional gridworlds and benchmark environments from Atari 2600 and MuJoCo. The method improves mean scores and exploration efficiency over the compared baselines on most tasks. These findings support diversity-driven training as a practical way to help policies avoid becoming trapped in local optima, with the reported advantage spanning several kinds of environments rather than every evaluated task.
neurips-2018-diversity-driven-exploratio.tldr: Adding an adaptively scaled diversity term improves exploration and scores over baselines on most evaluated reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Streaming inference must update predictions as observations arrive and identify when the process generating them changes. This paper introduces a robust Bayesian online changepoint detector using General Bayesian Inference with beta-divergences. Its robustness covers both the predictive distribution and the posterior over changepoints, which is the sense in which the procedure is doubly robust.

The authors provide a construction for exponential models and demonstrate it with Bayesian linear regression. To make the inference scalable, they use structural variational approximations that become exact as beta approaches zero. They also choose beta online by minimizing expected predictive loss, giving the divergence parameter a data-guided selection principle.

The resulting procedure has linear time and constant space complexity. On the reported real-world data, changepoint false discovery rates fall from values as high as 99% to 0%. This empirical result concerns avoiding false declarations of change in those evaluations. Alongside the computational properties, it supports robust treatment of both predictions and change decisions within a single streaming inference procedure.
neurips-2018-doubly-robust-bayesian-infe.tldr: Beta-divergence Bayesian inference robustifies streaming predictions and changepoint detection, sharply reducing false changepoint discoveries in reported data.

paragraphs: Large-vocabulary language models can devote most of their storage to the matrices that represent input words and generate output words. The abstract's bigLSTM example uses more than six gigabytes for these matrices, which contain over 90% of its parameters. GroupReduce targets this concentration of model size to make language models easier to serve under resource constraints.

The method groups words into blocks according to their frequency and compresses each block through a weighted low-rank approximation. It then iteratively refines the grouping. Word frequencies supply the weights, allowing the compression process to reflect the strongly uneven distribution of word usage instead of treating the entire vocabulary as one uniform matrix.

Experiments show stronger compression performance than the compared conventional low-rank and pruning methods. On the One-Billion-Word dataset, GroupReduce achieves 6.6-fold compression of the embedding and softmax matrices. Combining it with quantization yields 26-fold compression without losing prediction accuracy in the reported experiment. These figures apply specifically to the targeted matrices, demonstrating the value of frequency-aware compression where model storage is concentrated.
neurips-2018-groupreduce-block-wise-low-.tldr: GroupReduce uses frequency-aware blockwise low-rank approximation to compress language-model matrices, reaching 26-fold compression with quantization in the reported experiment.

paragraphs: Stimulus-driven brain-computer interfaces infer a user's intent from neural responses to a sequence of sensory events. The user attends to relevant targets within that sequence. Presentation schedules are typically pseudo-random, even though changing brain signals and current uncertainty suggest that some stimuli could be more informative than others at a particular moment.

This paper develops an information-based method for selecting stimuli adaptively. The computational obstacle is the large space of possible stimuli, which must be searched within strict real-time processing requirements. The authors reduce the objective to a single quantity: the prior probability mass associated with the stimulus under consideration, irrespective of its particular contents.

That reduction yields a simple analytical solution for the selection objective, making an otherwise high-dimensional decision more tractable. Simulations and real-time experiments with human participants demonstrate improvements in BCI performance. The contribution links uncertainty about user intent to stimulus scheduling, while providing a computational simplification that allows adaptive selection to operate within the interface's timing constraints.
neurips-2018-information-based-adaptive-.tldr: Reducing stimulus selection to a one-dimensional information objective enables adaptive BCI scheduling that improves performance in simulations and human experiments.

paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires a representation of how their parts fit together. This paper combines recurrent neural networks with tensor product representations to learn such combinatorial structure. The aim is to make the resulting representations easier to interpret symbolically and better able to generalize systematically when the arrangement of familiar information changes.

The architecture is trained end to end with gradient descent on several simple natural-language reasoning tasks. The authors evaluate it both when learning an individual task and when learning all tasks together. In both settings, they report substantial improvements over the latest state-of-the-art models used for comparison.

The paper also modifies a subset of the data so that training and test examples differ in large, systematic ways. The proposed approach generalizes better than the previous state of the art under this evaluation. That result supports the purpose of the representation design: learned combinations can help reasoning extend across structured differences between training and testing. The evidence concerns the simple reasoning tasks and altered data studied in the paper.
neurips-2018-learning-to-reason-with-thi.tldr: Combining recurrent networks with tensor product representations improves simple language reasoning and generalization across systematic data differences.

paragraphs: A system learning continuously must incorporate new experiences while preserving useful earlier knowledge. VASE, a variational autoencoder with shared embeddings, addresses this problem through unsupervised learning from visual data. Its setting is piecewise stationary: the data distribution remains stable for stretches of experience and then changes.

Using the Minimum Description Length principle, VASE automatically detects distribution shifts and assigns spare representational capacity to new knowledge. At the same time, it protects representations learned earlier from catastrophic forgetting. The approach encourages disentanglement, so different aspects of the data can receive more separable internal representations rather than becoming tightly mixed together.

The authors report several consequences of this organization. VASE handles ambiguous inputs sensibly, improves its representations through imagination-based exploration, and shares latent variables across datasets in semantically meaningful ways. Compared with baselines whose representations are entangled, it supports cross-domain inference beyond surface statistics. The contribution connects continual learning with reusable internal structure: preserving previous knowledge and discovering meaningful relationships between domains are treated as parts of the same representation-learning problem.
neurips-2018-life-long-disentangled-repr.tldr: VASE detects distribution shifts, preserves earlier representations, and shares meaningful latent structure across visual domains.

paragraphs: Repeated collection creates a privacy problem even when each individual collection uses a private algorithm. Applying a method designed for one use over many periods can weaken the overall guarantee until it becomes uninformative. This paper addresses that accumulation in the local differential privacy setting used by large-scale statistical collection systems.

The proposed technique maintains current statistics while making privacy degradation depend on the number of changes in the underlying distribution, rather than the number of collection periods. The distinction matters when measurements are frequent but the population's statistical behavior changes less often. Continued collection can then be analyzed in terms of actual distributional change.

The authors study users divided into an unknown set of groups. Each period, every user draws one bit from a changing distribution shared by their group. They apply the technique to tracking a statistic in this setting and also to frequency and heavy-hitter estimation. The result provides a framework for ongoing private monitoring whose privacy accounting reflects evolving data rather than simply counting repeated collection events.
neurips-2018-local-differential-privacy-.tldr: A local privacy technique ties long-term privacy degradation to distribution changes instead of the number of data collections.

paragraphs: The classic Mallows model describes probability distributions over complete rankings, represented as permutations. In practical settings, however, the available ranking may include only a leading subset of items. This paper extends the model to top-k lists, allowing the probabilistic object being modeled to match that partial-ranking form directly.

The extension uses a distance measure suited to comparing top-k lists. Choosing such a distance is central because the model needs a coherent way to express differences between these incomplete rankings. The authors develop a formulation that is both analytically tractable and computationally efficient, addressing two requirements that can be difficult to satisfy together.

They investigate sampling and reconstruction through both algorithms and experiments. These problems examine the model from complementary directions: generating lists according to it and recovering modeled structure from data. The contribution is therefore more than a definition of a distribution. It supplies an extension of Mallows with mathematical and computational tools for working with top-k observations, demonstrating that partial rankings can support a practical probabilistic modeling framework.
neurips-2018-mallows-models-for-top-k-li.tldr: A tractable extension of the Mallows model handles top-k rankings and supports efficient sampling and reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting a limited number of items to maximize a non-monotone submodular objective. Submodularity captures diminishing returns, while non-monotonicity allows an additional item to reduce the objective. The cardinality constraint limits the selection size. The central question is how to solve this class of problems with much less sequential dependence.

The authors give an algorithm with an approximation guarantee arbitrarily close to 1/(2e), using O(log² n) adaptive rounds for a ground set of n items. Adaptive rounds count stages that depend on results from earlier stages. Reducing their number allows more work to proceed in parallel, yielding an exponential improvement in parallel running time over previously studied algorithms for this constrained problem.

Experiments examine traffic monitoring and personalized data summarization. The algorithm produces objective values competitive with state-of-the-art methods while using exponentially fewer parallel iterations. The theoretical and empirical contributions emphasize the same tradeoff: obtaining useful solution quality while sharply reducing the sequential stages that limit parallel execution.
neurips-2018-non-monotone-submodular-max.tldr: A non-monotone submodular maximization algorithm achieves a near-1/(2e) approximation in O(log² n) adaptive rounds.

paragraphs: Batch normalization is widely used to improve neural-network training, but its benefits and shortcomings motivate a closer look at what normalization actually does. This paper interprets normalization and weight decay as ways to separate the magnitude of weights from the objective being optimized. That perspective connects normalization choices with weight decay and learning-rate adjustments.

The authors propose alternatives to conventional L2 batch normalization using L1 and L-infinity normalization. Changing the norm changes the numerical operations involved in normalization. The proposed alternatives can substantially improve numerical stability in low-precision implementations while also offering computational and memory benefits, making the choice relevant to how training is implemented.

The paper demonstrates methods that enable what it describes as the first batch-normalization alternative to work in half precision. It also modifies weight normalization and reports improved performance on large-scale tasks. Together, these contributions combine an interpretation of weight magnitude during optimization with concrete normalization designs, showing how mathematical choices about scale can influence both training behavior and implementation efficiency.
neurips-2018-norm-matters-efficient-and-.tldr: A weight-scale perspective motivates alternative normalization schemes with low-precision stability, efficiency, and performance benefits.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many different functions neuronal models can implement. It defines capacity as the logarithm of that number, or of the corresponding volume when volume is the relevant measure. The resulting quantity describes the range of functions available to a model and provides a common language for comparing different neuronal constructions.

The authors review established results and derive new capacity estimates for several types of individual neurons. These include linear and polynomial threshold gates, versions with binary or positive weight constraints, and ReLU neurons. Considering constrained weights alongside other models brings restrictions on parameter choices into the same analysis of representational possibilities.

The study also extends to fully recurrent and layered feedforward networks, deriving capacity estimates and bounds for these architectures. Its contribution is a collection of mathematical characterizations spanning both individual computational units and networks of units. Through the chosen capacity definition, the paper connects neuron type, weight restrictions, and network organization to the size of the function family each construction can represent.
neurips-2018-on-neuronal-capacity-d2f1b4.tldr: The paper estimates neuronal and network capacity by measuring the size of the function families they can implement.

paragraphs: Some learning and signal-processing tasks can be expressed as minimizing a convex function whose argument is a measure. Examples include sparse spike deconvolution and training a neural network with one hidden layer. This paper studies what happens when that measure is represented by a collection of particles with adjustable weights and positions.

The optimization method moves those weights and positions through continuous-time gradient descent. This particle formulation is non-convex even though the original objective is convex in the measure. It also provides an idealized description of training a network with a large hidden layer. The authors analyze the dynamics using Wasserstein gradient flows from optimal transport theory.

They prove convergence to global minimizers when initialization is appropriate and the number of particles tends to infinity. Both conditions are part of the guarantee. Numerical experiments indicate that the asymptotic behavior already appears with a reasonable finite particle count, including in high dimensions. The result connects over-parameterized optimization to a measure-based formulation that makes its global behavior mathematically accessible.
neurips-2018-on-the-global-convergence-o.tldr: With appropriate initialization, particle gradient flow converges globally in the many-particle limit for the studied measure-based optimization problems.

paragraphs: Approximate Bayesian computation supports Bayesian inference when the likelihood is too difficult to evaluate directly. Existing sampling-based approaches can become inefficient with high-dimensional parameters, while regression-based alternatives can be difficult to scale. This paper introduces an optimization-based framework intended to address both obstacles through a different formulation of the inference problem.

The method uses a generative model to match posterior and joint distributions. The authors show that this matching task can be expressed as saddle-point optimization, with objectives accessible directly from samples. This gives a route from simulated or sampled information to an optimization problem without requiring direct evaluation of the intractable likelihood.

They develop predictive approximate Bayesian computation, or P-ABC, and provide a probabilistically approximately correct bound guaranteeing learning consistency. A numerical experiment reports significant improvements over K2-ABC and DR-ABC. The contribution combines a sample-accessible optimization formulation, an algorithm built from it, and theoretical support for its learning behavior, with empirical evidence against the two named alternatives.
neurips-2018-predictive-approximate-baye.tldr: P-ABC formulates likelihood-intractable Bayesian inference as sample-based saddle-point optimization with a learning-consistency guarantee.

paragraphs: Hypothesis testing chooses between competing explanations for observations, but the distributions associated with those explanations may be uncertain. This paper represents that uncertainty using sets centered on empirical distributions. Wasserstein distance determines which nearby distributions belong to each set, providing a data-driven construction without assuming a particular distributional family.

The authors formulate robust testing as a minimax problem and develop a safe convex approximation. They show that the approximation yields a nearly optimal detector within the family of all possible tests. This turns protection against unfavorable distributions into an optimization problem with a more manageable computational form.

By exploiting the structure of a least favorable distribution, they further derive a tractable reformulation. Its complexity is independent of observation dimension and can be nearly independent of sample size in general. A real-data example involving human activity demonstrates strong detector performance. The contribution combines distributional robustness with computational accessibility, addressing both uncertainty about the hypotheses and the practical cost of constructing a test.
neurips-2018-robust-hypothesis-testing-u.tldr: Wasserstein uncertainty sets yield a data-driven robust testing framework with a tractable approximation and near-optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: A large semidefinite program can be made smaller by representing its matrix variable as X = YY*, with Y having relatively few columns. This automatically enforces positive semidefiniteness and reduces the number of optimization variables. The price is non-convexity, raising the question of whether solutions reached in the factorized problem are good.

Earlier results established global optimality of exact second-order stationary points under smoothness and rank conditions for almost all cost matrices. Practical algorithms, however, generally produce only approximate stationary points. This paper addresses the gap between an exact mathematical condition and the approximate conditions a numerical method can satisfy.

Under similar assumptions, the authors use smoothed analysis to show that approximate second-order stationary points of a randomly perturbed objective are approximately globally optimal. The required factor width scales like the square root of the number of constraints, up to logarithmic factors. They also specialize the results to a semidefinite relaxation of phase retrieval. The guarantee supports approximate computation while explicitly retaining the perturbation and structural assumptions.
neurips-2018-smoothed-analysis-of-the-lo.tldr: Under structural assumptions and random objective perturbation, approximate stationary points of low-rank SDP formulations are approximately globally optimal.

paragraphs: Backpropagation sends error gradients backward through a network in sequence. This creates backward locking: a layer must wait for information from later layers before it can update. The dependency limits parallel use of computing resources. Earlier attempts to decouple training face substantial accuracy loss or excessive memory requirements as networks become deep.

This paper proposes a parallel-objective formulation of neural-network training and introduces the features replay algorithm based on that formulation. The authors prove convergence to critical points of the non-convex problem under certain conditions. Critical-point convergence is the stated theoretical outcome; the guarantee does not identify those points as global optima.

The method is evaluated by training deep convolutional neural networks. Relative to the compared methods, the experiments show faster convergence, lower memory consumption, and better generalization error. These results address the practical difficulties motivating the work: parallel training must reduce sequential dependencies without making memory use or predictive performance unacceptable. The paper combines a reformulated objective, a conditional convergence result, and evidence of benefits in deep-network training.
neurips-2018-training-neural-networks-us.tldr: Features replay enables parallel-oriented neural-network training with conditional critical-point convergence and reported speed, memory, and generalization benefits.

paragraphs: Neural networks with different architectures can be very different in how easily they train, while training settings can affect how well the resulting models generalize. This paper investigates those differences through the geometry of the loss function. The aim is to make aspects of a highly non-convex optimization problem visible and comparable.

The authors introduce filter normalization as a method for visualizing loss curvature and making meaningful side-by-side comparisons between loss functions. A comparison method matters because the goal is to study differences across networks and training choices, rather than simply produce an isolated picture of one model's loss.

Using several visualization techniques, the paper explores how architecture affects the landscape and how batch size, learning rate, and optimizer choices affect the shape around minimizers. It also examines the relationship between landscape structure and generalization. The contribution is an investigative framework for connecting design and training decisions to observable loss geometry, helping organize questions about why some networks train more easily and some learned solutions generalize better.
neurips-2018-visualizing-the-loss-landsc.tldr: Filter-normalized visualizations help compare how network architectures and training choices shape neural-network loss landscapes.
